headline: Stellwagen Edge in 110 to 140 feet: cod holding the gravel, bluefin still riding the whale sign
subhead: Groundfish are settled into their September lanes and the tuna haven't left the mackerel yet — here's where the effort is paying off.
body_markdown:
One-ten to one-forty feet of water on the Stellwagen Edge is where the boats are finding their bottom this week, and that gravel is holding cod the way it's supposed to in mid-September — not a blitz, but a steady, dependable pick for anyone willing to work the drift correctly. Push north into the Basin and the depth stretches out to 180, 200 feet of soft mud, and that's where the haddock have been stacking up, mixed with pollock on the up-current side of the drop-offs. This is the pattern the Bank runs every fall once the water starts easing off its summer peak, and so far this year it's tracking true to form.

The wind's been the bigger variable than the fish. A string of moderate southwest breezes early in the week kept the chop workable but made anchoring tough on the gravel patches — boats that stuck with drift-fishing did better than the ones trying to hold bottom on a single mark. That should ease into the weekend as the wind backs around more northerly, which will flatten the swell on the Edge and make the anchor-and-chum game viable again for the haddock crowd working the Basin mud. Watch the moon — we're coming off the new phase, so tide swings have been building through the week, and the stronger push has actually helped concentrate bait over the humps rather than spreading it thin.

Mackerel remain thick on top of the Bank, and that's the story driving everything else right now, groundfish and tuna both. Where you find diving birds and slicks of mackerel scales on the surface, cod and pollock are usually stacked underneath working the same bait pushed down against the gravel. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid through those mackerel schools has been putting cod in the 8 to 15-pound class in the boat, along with a good number of pollock mixed in on the faster retrieve. For the bottom bite proper, standard cod rigs — a two-hook rig baited with clam or squid, fished tight to the gravel edges in that 110 to 140-foot band — have been the more consistent producer for the boats not wanting to burn arms on jigs all day.

Haddock fishing on the mud has been the more reliable of the two grounds fish patterns this week. Fleets working the Basin in that 180 to 200-foot range, anchored or slow-drifting with clam bait on standard haddock rigs, have been finding decent numbers of fish in the 2 to 4-pound class, with the occasional larger fish mixed through. Hake have shown up as a bycatch on the same drops, mostly on the deeper edges where the mud transitions to broken bottom — not a target fishery for most boats, but worth keeping bait down if you're grinding for haddock and want something to show for a slow stretch.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefin would stay in reach on the Bank as long as the bait held, and that's exactly what's playing out. Whale activity has been consistent over the mackerel schools on top of Stellwagen, and where you find the whales working, the tuna have been showing not far behind, coming up on the same bait from below. The pattern has been classic September Gulf of Maine — cooler water keeping things honest, no warm-water surprises pushing exotic species into the mix, just bluefin doing what bluefin do when the forage is stacked this thick. Trolling spreads of green machines and small feathers over the Edge and along Tillies Bank have connected with fish in the 60 to 100-inch class this week, with the better window running early morning before the wind builds and again in the last two hours of light when the mackerel push tight to the surface.

Carter Canyon and the approach out toward Cape Cod Tails haven't produced much chatter this week — that water's still a bit ahead of the season for consistent action, and most of the fleet's attention has stayed concentrated on the Bank itself where the bait is. No sense running the extra miles when the tuna are sitting right on top of Stellwagen chasing mackerel the whales are already pointing you toward.

Looking at the next few days, the backing wind should open up better conditions for both fisheries. If the northerly holds through the weekend, expect the gravel bite on the Edge to stay steady on jigs and bait rigs alike, and the haddock on the mud should improve further as boats get back to anchoring cleanly instead of fighting a southwest chop. For the tuna, the call is simple: find the whales, find the mackerel balls, and work that water early before the day's wind builds a groundswell that pushes the bait deeper and scatters the surface activity. If the mackerel start thinning out on top — which typically happens as water temperatures ease further into fall — expect the bluefin to follow that bait down and the visible surface bite to get tougher to find, even if the fish are still around. For now, the pattern's holding, and the Bank is fishing the way it should this time of year.
